I can’t find the link

Get the link for a Facebook profile, Page, group or event

  1. Enter the name of the profile, Page, group or event in the search box at the top of any page on Facebook, and click Search.
  2. Click the name of the profile, Page, group or event you’re trying to report.
  3. Copy the link (URL) found in your browser’s address bar.

Get the link for a specific piece of content created by a profile, Page, group or event (example: comment, photo)

  1. Click the date or time link in the post, comment, photo, share or video.
  2. Copy the link in your browser’s address bar.

Help and support for suicidal or self-injurious thoughts

Find a suicide helpline

Help for self-injury

Help for eating disorders

If you’re in immediate physical danger, please contact local law enforcement or a suicide helpline for help.

If you’re going through something difficult and the threat isn’t immediate, we want you to know there are things you can do right now that may help you.

Talk to someone at a helpline

Suicide Prevention

  • Find your local suicide helpline by viewing our full list of prevention resources. We partner with over 50 expert organizations around the world.

Self-Injury

  • In the US, United Kingdom and Ireland, contact Reach Out: 1-800-448-3000; L (l.facebook.com)
  • In Australia, contact headspace: 1800 650 890; L (l.facebook.com)
  • In other countries, contact Befrienders: 1-800-448-3000; L (l.facebook.com).

Eating Disorders

  • In the US, contact the National Eating Disorders Association: 1-800-931-2237; info@myneda.org; L (l.facebook.com).
  • Take a free, anonymous online assessment to help you understand your risk of an eating disorder.

Reach out to someone you trust

Contact someone you trust, like a family member, friend, counselor or teacher, and ask them to let you share what’s on your mind. For example, you could say, “I’m going through something difficult and was hoping to talk to you about it. If that’s OK with you, can you take some time to listen?”

## Learn about other ways to support yourself

It can be difficult to focus when you’re overwhelmed or can’t find a solution to a problem right away. Stop for a moment, take a deep breath and give yourself a break from your feelings.

Try some of these tips from self-care experts at Forefront and the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline.

Change your surroundings:

  • Go for a walk outside if you can.

  • Let in some fresh air by opening a window or a door.

  • Try sitting in a different room, on a doorstep or even just facing a different direction. Be creative:

  • Draw something simple.

  • Make a nice meal.

  • Write a short story. Soothe your senses:

  • Meditate or do yoga.

  • Take a hot shower.

  • Listen to your favorite songs. Relax:

  • Look at the clouds.

  • Read a book, magazine or blog post.

  • Take a nap.

If the tips above don’t work for you, see more things you can do right now.

You can also learn more about dealing with suicidal thoughts and find local self-care experts.

If you have a friend who’s having thoughts about suicide or self-injury, you can share these resources with them as well.

How community notes work on Facebook

Become a contributor

What are contributor requirements?

I can’t write a note

What happens to my post?

Community Notes on Facebook is currently in beta and some features might be unavailable.

If you find a bug while Community Notes is still in beta, you can report it by shaking your phone.

Community notes are written by contributors on Facebook, Instagram and Threads to help keep you better informed about a post that might be misleading or confusing. A community note may be shown on the post if enough contributors with different views have agreed that it’s helpful.

How to participate

Anyone on Facebook, Instagram and Threads can view a community note on a post. Notes can appear on any content viewable by people in the United States, regardless of where the creator is located. Only contributors can write a community note or rate other contributors’ notes as helpful or not helpful. Meta does not decide which community notes get rated or published.

To become a contributor, you must meet the following requirements:

  • Be at least 18 years old.
  • Have a Facebook, Instagram or Threads account that’s at least 6 months old. On Facebook, both personal profiles and Pages can participate as Community Notes contributors.
  • Have a verified phone number or have two-factor authentication enabled.
  • Have an account that hasn’t repeatedly broken Meta’s rules.
  • Have joined the waitlist to be a contributor on Facebook.

Note: Contributors can sign up for each app. Visit the Instagram Help Center to learn how to join the waitlist for Instagram and Threads.

Keep in mind:

  • Community notes won’t have author names attached. That means people on Facebook, Instagram or Threads can’t see the name or photo of the contributor who wrote a note. They also can’t see the names or photos of the contributors who rated the note helpful.
  • Names and photos of contributors will be visible to Meta’s internal systems to ensure that community notes follow Meta’s Community Standards.
  • Details that contributors choose to include in their community note could reveal their identity.

How community notes work

How to write and rate notes

How rating works

How matching works

Impact on speech

Meta’s platforms are built to be places where people can express themselves freely. When a community note appears on a post, it won’t affect who can see that content or how widely it can be shared. If a community note appears on your post, you will receive a notification. You won’t be able to remove the note.

Meta may still remove content that goes against the Community Standards. It may also remove misinformation when it could lead to physical harm or could interfere with an election or civic process.

How do I report a problem with Facebook and the assistive technology I’m using?

Report assistive technology problem

What to include in my report?

My screen reader isn’t working

If you’re experiencing a problem using assistive technology settings like screen readers, magnification tools or alternate input methods with Facebook, please log into Facebook and send us accessibility feedback.

Before you report

If you’re experiencing issues with Facebook that aren’t related to assistive technology, learn how to report a problem with Facebook.

If you’re using a mobile device, make sure the operating system and Facebook app are current. Updating the app and operating system may solve the problem. You can check the versions in the Settings app for your device.

When you report an issue, include information about your device, the assistive technology that you’re using and what you were doing on Facebook when the problem occurred. Including this information helps us recreate the problem.

What to include in your report

Information about your device:

  • Brand
  • Model
  • Operating system

For example, Apple iPhone 12 with iOS 14.5.1 or Google Pixel 5 with Android 11.

Information about the assistive technology or assistive technology setting:

  • Name
  • Version number
  • Feature you’re using

Information about what you were doing on Facebook:

  • Facebook product or feature
  • Facebook URL
  • Steps you took when the problem occured

How Facebook selects independent fact-checkers

Who are fact-checkers?

How are fact-checkers selected?

What is the Code of Principles?

We’re only partnering with independent fact-checkers in select countries right now.

How Facebook uses artificial intelligence to moderate content

How AI moderates content?

What are Community Standards?

Request content review

How AI learns decisions?

When we find content (example: post, comment, story) that goes against our Community Standards, we remove it from Facebook. If the content doesn’t go against our Community Standards but may be inappropriate, disrespectful, or offensive, we may do things like reduce the distribution of the content on Facebook or mark it as sensitive. Our Community Standards define what is and isn’t allowed on Facebook, and they apply all over the world. They’re designed to encourage expression and create a safe environment on Facebook.

To find, review, and take action on content that may go against our Community Standards, we use technology and human reviewers. Artificial intelligence (AI) technology is central to our content review process. AI can detect and remove content that goes against our Community Standards before anyone reports it. Other times, our technology sends content to human review teams to take a closer look and make a decision on it. These thousands of reviewers around the world focus on content that is most harmful to Facebook users.

How artificial intelligence makes decisions about content

AI teams start by building machine learning models that can do things like recognize what’s in a photo or analyze the text of a post. For example, AI models may be built to learn whether a piece of content contains nudity or graphic content. Those models may then determine whether to take action on the content, such as removing it from the platform or reducing its distribution.

Sometimes, a piece of content requires further review and our AI sends it to a human review team to take a closer look. In these cases, review teams make the final decision, and our technology learns and improves from each decision. Over time—after learning from thousands of human decisions—the technology gets better.

Our policies may change over time to keep up with changes in social norms, language and our products and services. As a result, our content review process constantly evolves.

If we’ve taken down a piece of your content that you don’t believe goes against our Community Standards, you can request a review.

Visit our Transparency Center to learn more about how we use technology and review teams to detect, review, and take action on content.

How is Facebook addressing false information through independent fact-checkers?

My post was fact-checked

Appeal a fact-checker rating

How to spot false information

Report false information

We’re committed to fighting the spread of false information on Facebook. In certain countries, we work with independent fact-checkers who are certified through the non-partisan International Fact-Checking Network to help identify and review false information. Fact-checkers check the facts and rate the accuracy of information.

[Embedded video omitted]

0:00 / 2:33

Reducing the distribution of false information

  • Showing false information lower in Feed: If a fact-checker rates a photo, video, text or link as false, it will be moved lower in Feed. This significantly reduces the number of people who are likely to see it.
  • Taking action against repeat offenders: Pages and websites that repeatedly share false information will see their distribution reduced and their ability to advertise removed.
  • Using technology to find copies of false information: Each piece of information might have thousands of copies across Facebook, and they might have small differences like a different photo crop. We use machine-learning technology to detect these copies so that fact-checkers can focus on new information.
  • Reducing repeatedly fact-checked claims: We use technology and a review team to detect when a post contains particular common, widespread claims that multiple fact-checkers have said are false.

Providing more information if you see false information

  • Providing more context on false information: When fact-checkers write articles with more information, you’ll see a notice where you can click to see why.
  • Notifying people who shared false information: You’ll receive a notification if you try to share a post that includes false information or have shared one in the past. Page admins will also be notified if they share posts with false information.
  • Rating options for fact-checkers: Learn more about rating options for independent fact-checkers as well as some guidelines and examples for content that is likely to fit within each rating.

Giving you ways to identify and give feedback on false information

  • Learn how to spot false information. Knowing what to look out for can help you make more informed decisions about what to read, trust, and share.
  • Provide feedback on posts you think are false. Let us know if you think a post is false. This is one of the signs we use when trying to identify false information.
  • Appeal a fact-checker’s rating on your content: Let fact-checkers know if you corrected the content they rated or you think a fact-check got something wrong about your content.

How matching works for community notes on Facebook

How do notes match?

What posts get notes?

Why didn’t my note match?

To help more people see Community Notes, we’re starting to apply published notes to similar posts which are identical (they include the same caption and image or video) or are nearly identical (they include the same image or video). We do this only if contributors agree these notes should apply to matched content.

If our systems detect identical or nearly identical posts, we’ll ask contributors if they think the same note should be added to them. If enough contributors from the community also agree that the notes should be added to the identical or nearly-identical posts, we will add the notes to them. This step helps ensure that we aren’t matching notes to irrelevant posts with the same media.

How does matching work?

  1. Contributors add notes to posts which people have requested them on.
  2. Other contributors rate these notes as helpful or not helpful.
  3. As part of the rating process, if our systems detect identical or nearly identical posts, we’ll ask contributors if they think the note should be added to them.
  4. Contributors can see the identical or nearly identical posts which have been detected at the time of rating, and say yes or no on whether the note should be added to all identical posts before they submit their rating.
  5. Post authors who receive a matched note will be notified.

After a note is matched

If a note is matched to an identical or nearly identical post and published on Feed, people can select About this note to see the other posts it appears on.

How rating works for community notes on Facebook

What is consensus?

Note status meanings

My note status changed

Community Notes is a feature designed to publish notes that are helpful to the widest range of people by considering not just the number of contributors who rate a note as helpful or unhelpful, but also whether those contributors represent different perspectives. When this happens, we say that a note has reached consensus.

Why consensus matters

Consensus means that a diverse group of contributors—people with different perspectives and rating histories (example: they’ve rated notes differently in the past)—agree that a note adds valuable context to a post. This helps ensure that notes are not biased and reflect a broad understanding of the topic.

Requiring agreement from people with different perspectives helps ensure notes are fair and not one-sided.

Note statuses

In your Community Notes home, you’ll see notes with a few different statuses:

  • Needs more ratings: This means the note hasn’t reached consensus.
  • People agreed this note is helpful: This means the note has reached a “helpful” consensus, and is (or may soon be) published on the post.
  • People agreed this note is not helpful: This means the note has reached a “not helpful” consensus, and isn’t published anywhere.

To learn more about the status of a note, the author and how people rated it, you select Options on the note.

The consensus status of a note can change

As more contributors review and rate notes, or as new information becomes available, the status of a note may change. If you want to contribute, focus on providing clear, factual, and neutral information—this increases the chances that your note will reach consensus and be published.

How Safety Check is activated on Facebook

How is Safety Check activated?

Mark myself safe

What triggers Safety Check?

When an incident such as an earthquake, hurricane, mass shooting or building collapse occurs where people might be in danger, global crisis reporting agencies alert Facebook.

Safety Check will be activated when people in the affected area post about the incident. Once Safety Check is activated, people in the area may receive a notification from Facebook to mark themselves safe. People who click the Safety Check notification will also be able to see if any of their friends are in the affected area or have marked themselves safe.

How security keys work on Facebook

Add a security key

Log in with a security key

I lost my security key

What is a security key?

If you’re looking for help with keeping your account secure, follow these tips.

Learn about security keys and how they work

A security key is a small hardware device which can be used to help keep your Facebook account secure. Security keys are a method of two-factor authentication that adds a layer of security to logging in, often used on top of other two-factor authentication methods like text message (SMS) codes or a third-party authentication app.

Adding a security key is one of the best ways to keep your account secure because when the key is in your physical possession, only you can authorize a login to your account, even if the password is entered correctly. After you register a security key to your account, login attempts from an unrecognized browser or untrusted device will be prompted to physically authorize the login attempt via your security key.

To add a security key to your account, you’ll first need to purchase your own third party Universal 2nd Factor (U2F) or FIDO2 security key. Some types of keys can be used by inserting them into a USB or lightning port. Other types of keys can be used by holding them near your computer or mobile device. Before purchasing, make sure that your security key is compatible with the browser and the device that you use to log into your account.

Add a security key to your account or log in with one

You can get started by learning how to add a security key to your account. If you’ve already added a key to your account, you can learn how to log in with your key.

Avoid getting locked out of your account if you lose your security key

To make sure that you are not locked out of your account if you lose your security key, you’ll need to set up an additional backup two-factor authentication security method. The most secure method is to set up multiple keys for your account. If you don’t have a second key, you can enroll in another two-factor authentication security method such as text message (SMS) codes or a third-party authentication app.

Authenticate a login attempt on a browser or device that doesn’t support security keys

Security keys are only supported by certain browsers (Chrome, Opera, Firefox, Edge, or Safari) and mobile devices. If you want to be able to authorize a login attempt from a browser or device that doesn’t support security keys, you’ll have to set up an additional backup two-factor authentication security method such as text message (SMS) codes or a third-party authentication app.

What happens if you lose your security key?

Security keys are not a replacement for your password. If your key is lost or stolen, the person in possession of your key will not be able to log into your account without also knowing your username and password.

To make sure that you are not locked out of your account if you lose your security key, you’ll need to set up an additional backup two-factor authentication security method. The most secure method is to set up multiple keys for your account. If you don’t have a second key, you can enroll in another two-factor authentication security method such as text message (SMS) codes or a third-party authentication app.

Other useful resources

  • Your security key can be used with other websites while also being used for your Facebook account.
  • If you’re having trouble adding or using your security key, try clearing your cache and temporary data. You can also try restarting your computer or mobile device.
  • If you’re running Linux, you’ll need to follow this additional step to use your security key.

How to write and rate community notes on Facebook

Write a community note

Rate a community note

Find my notes

I can’t write a note

If you’re a contributor, you can add a community note to public posts you find in your Feed on Facebook, Instagram and Threads. Some content isn’t eligible for community notes like ads, reels, stories, and posts with limited audiences.

Writing a note

  1. Open Facebook on your device.
  2. Click Menu in the top right of Facebook.
  3. Select Community Notes.
  4. Click Write notes from the left to find a posts that could use helpful context.
  5. Add any additional information or helpful context.
    • Notes must be less than 500 characters.
    • Only include links or URLs in the source section.
  6. Add a link to a source that supports your note.
    • It’s required to add a link, and it will be shown with the community note
    • Including a link to a specific page or article can help increase your chances of getting a helpful rating from other contributors.
    • You can only add one link to your note.
  7. Select Submit to make your community note available for other contributors to rate its helpfulness. A submitted community note won’t be seen until enough contributors agree that it’s helpful.

Note: You can also write community notes from your Facebook Feed by selecting the Menu. You won’t be able to edit your note after you submit it.

Rating a note

  1. Open Facebook on your device.
  2. Click Menu in the top right of Facebook.
  3. Select Community Notes.
  4. Click Rate notes from the left to see community notes that contributors on Facebook submitted.
  5. Read the post and the community note submitted for the post, and select Helpful if the note provides helpful context, or Not helpful if the note doesn’t provide helpful context.
  6. Check the boxes for why you think the note is or isn’t helpful, then select Rate.
    • You can’t change or remove your rating.

Note: You can only rate community notes from the same app you’re currently using (example: When rating community notes from Facebook, you’ll only see Facebook notes).

Find your notes and ratings

You can view the community notes you’ve rated and created from the Your ratings and Your notes tab from the left.

From here you can see if other contributors have rated your note and the reasons they selected. You can also delete your community note from this tab. Nobody will be able to see or rate your deleted note, and any ratings on the note will be lost.

Learn more about the Meta Safety Advisory Council

What is the Safety Advisory Council?

Who is on the Safety Advisory Council?

How is the Council funded?

What is a non-disclosure agreement?

The Meta Safety Advisory Council is comprised of leading internet safety organizations from around the world. Meta consults with these organizations on issues related to online safety. Council members provide expertise, perspective and insights that inform our approach to safety.

Independence and Scope

Meta’s Safety Advisory Council is made up of independent online safety organizations and experts. Members provide expertise, perspective and insights that inform Meta’s approach to safety. They do not act as spokespeople for Meta, and they are not responsible for, or to be held accountable for, review of every policy, product, tool, feature or company announcement. Nor is the Safety Advisory Council designed to examine topics or subjects that fall outside safety (e.g., algorithms, brand trust, artificial intelligence), except if and where there are points of intersection.

Funding

Meta may on occasion provide grants and funding in support of the mission and core objectives of various online safety organizations, including all the members of its Safety Advisory Council. Meta and the receiving expert or organization will be transparent about whether funding has been granted to an expert or organization. Safety Advisory Council members may refuse funding for any reason and it will not impact their membership on the Council.

Non-Disclosure Agreement

On occasion, when seeking the guidance of the Safety Advisory Council, Meta shares confidential information, such as information about future product launches, with the council’s members. Members sign a non-disclosure agreement. The agreement does not constrain the Safety Advisory Council’s members from openly expressing their broader views about Meta, no matter how critical, so long as they do not share confidential information.

Centre for Social Research (CSR)

Centre for Social Research (CSR) is an India-based nonprofit working on women’s empowerment by conducting field research, providing capacity building and trainings, and advocating for legislative change. CSR actively uses social media to drive powerful social change campaigns and recently launched #SocialSurfing to train young people on safe, respectful and responsible usage of social media. Visit CSR at L (l.facebook.com).

Childnet International

Childnet International is a UK-based charity working domestically and internationally to help make the internet a safe place for children and young people, enabling them to use interactive technologies safely and responsibly. Childnet International has developed a number of resources designed to help young people and parents assess and manage the risks they may encounter online. Visit Childnet International at L (l.facebook.com).

Connect Safely

ConnectSafely.org is a leading interactive resource on the internet for parents, teens, educators and everyone engaged and interested in online safety for youth. Visit Connect Safely at L (l.facebook.com).

Insight SA

Insight is group of experts working together to educate and empower children online, and promote and protect their rights. The organization works in multi-stakeholder partnership with institutions, industry, national governments, universities and NGOs worldwide to develop educational tools and services to empower young people as responsible digital citizens. Visit Insight SA at L (l.facebook.com).

iWIN

iWIN (Institute of Watch Internet Network) is a non-profit organization created by Taiwan’s Protection of Children and Youths Welfare and Rights Act. Established in 2013, iWIN’s mission is to protect the children and youth from harmful contents on the internet through promoting digital literacy and industrywide self-regulation. iWIN serves as a platform for stakeholders from partner NGOs, subject matter experts, industry and relevant government bodies to jointly create a safer and informed online environment. Visit iWIN at L (l.facebook.com).

National Network to End Domestic Violence (NNEDV)

The Safety Net Project of the US National Network to End Domestic Violence (NNEDV) is a leader in online safety for survivors of domestic violence, dating abuse, cyber-stalking and harassment. Based in Washington DC, NNEDV represents coalitions against domestic violence in every US state and territory and works to address technology and safety with sister organizations worldwide. Visit NNEDV at L (l.facebook.com).

Net Family News

NetFamilyNews.org, a project of The Net Safety Collaborative (TNSC), is a blog that documents developments in the digital technology and media young people love and use most. In addition to its writing and consulting work, the organization has advised social media companies on digital safety and literacy for nearly a decade. Visit Net Family News at L (l.facebook.com).

Netsafe

Netsafe is New Zealand’s independent, non-profit online safety organisation. Netsafe provides online safety education, advice and support for New Zealand internet users. Taking a technology-positive approach to the challenges digital technology presents, Netsafe works to help people in New Zealand take advantage of the opportunities available through technology by providing practical tools, support and advice for managing online challenges. Visit Netsafe at L (l.facebook.com).

PROJECT ROCKIT

PROJECT ROCKIT is Australia’s youth-driven movement against bullying, hate and prejudice online. PROJECT ROCKIT is all about creating spaces where young people have access to respect, acceptance, creative expression and real social leadership. Since 2006, their workshops have helped young people celebrate technology, combat online hate and stand up to bullying instead of standing by. Through face-to-face workshops, an online curriculum and a digital program, ‘PROJECT ROCKIT TV’, hundreds of thousands of young people have been impacted and are mobilized to stand up and lead change. Visit PROJECT ROCKIT at L (l.facebook.com).

SaferNet Brazil

SaferNet Brazil is a non-profit organization founded in 2005 that focuses on building research and social projects to combat Human Rights violations online. Working together with civil society, industry, the government and law enforcement authorities, SaferNet aims to make the internet a responsible and ethical environment that allows children and adults to create, develop and build social relationships, knowledge and citizenship in a safe manner. Visit Safernet Brazil at L (l.facebook.com).

Manage restored content on Facebook

Update audience settings

If you posted content (posts, pictures, videos) using an app or website that uses your Facebook login, and that app or website was deleted or disabled, the posted content may have been hidden on Facebook.

In some instances, apps and websites were removed from Facebook for integrity reasons or violating Facebook’s Terms of Service. In these cases, the content associated with those apps and websites was also hidden.

To give you access and control over your personal information and content, some of your previously hidden content may have been recently restored to your Facebook account.

If you would like to archive or delete this content from your account, you can do so at any time. You can also update the audience settings for the restored content at any time.

When content is restored to your Facebook account:

  • The restored post will reappear on your timeline at the day and time of its original publication.
  • In most cases, restored content will automatically use the only me audience option. For content restored from features that do not have the only me setting, such as content from Pages, content will be restored to the most conservative setting available for that feature. Once the content is restored you can update the audience settings at any time.
  • If you previously tagged other Facebook users in restored content, and the tags no longer appear, you can choose to re-tag them after the content is restored.
  • Restored content that you posted to another Facebook user’s timeline may have a different audience setting than only me depending on that user’s audience settings. You can choose to delete these posts at any time.
  • Content that other users posted to your timeline may become hidden when it’s restored, even if it was not previously hidden. You can unhide this content at any time.

Note: If you create or post new content using a third-party app that is later deleted by the developer, that content may temporarily disappear.

Protect yourself from phishing on Facebook

My account was phished

What is phishing?

Avoid phishing links

Signs of phishing

We have seen evidence of malicious actors sending Business Manager partner requests that include phishing links. As we investigate this issue, we encourage you to exercise caution as these notifications come from a legitimate Meta domain (facebookmail.com). If you don’t know the person or business mentioned in the partner request, do not click on any links.

You can take steps to protect yourself from phishing scams on Facebook.

Find what to do if you think you’ve been phished.

What is phishing?

Phishing is when someone tries to trick you into giving up your personal information, like passwords or credit card numbers, often by sending you online communications (such as email or messages) that are designed to look legitimate. Phishing attacks can come in many different forms, but a common phishing attack example is when someone sends you deceptive links. These links may appear harmless, but if you click on them, they can lead you to dangerous or fraudulent websites that look legitimate, where your personal information or login credentials can be stolen.

Scammers and bad actors online may use phishing techniques to try to steal your login information or to infect your device with malware. Additionally, when bad actors take control over an account or device, they will sometimes use that account to send spam or inappropriate content to other people you may know, including friends or family.

Phishing attacks are particularly harmful because they don’t remain isolated to one online service or app. Clicking on one fraudulent link can lead to bad actors taking over multiple accounts (like your email account, Facebook account, Whatsapp account, etc.) or devices, which can then be used to phish your family or friends. Phishing does not only take place on Facebook, it’s an issue you need to be aware of across all online platforms and apps you may use.

Example of phishing on Facebook

You read a post on Facebook from someone you think you know, informing you that a famous person has died. When you click the link in their post, you are taken to a fake Facebook login page where you unknowingly give your account credentials to scammers. These scammers then take over your account and hold it hostage, demanding money or spamming your Facebook contacts with inappropriate content.

Signs that your Facebook account may have been phished

  • You can’t access your Facebook account.
  • Your friends or family tell you that they are receiving inappropriate messages, videos, or images from your account.
  • You are now following people or pages you don’t want to follow.
  • Other accounts of yours, such as those from financial institutions or email services, are compromised.

Tips to avoid phishing attacks on your Facebook account

  • Don’t click on links or open attachments from unknown sources. Instead, report it to phish@fb.com. If you’re a business, go to Meta Business Support Home to review your account status and note any support issues. Avoid clicking on links within any unsolicited messages, whether it’s email, Messenger, or text, even if they appear to be from Facebook. Always be cautious and avoid opening attachments from unfamiliar businesses or individuals. Remember, even your friends or family may unknowingly send you malicious attachments, especially if their account has already been compromised.

  • Be on the lookout for signs of phishing, such as misspelled words, bad grammar, or design mistakes in messages. These errors could signal that something is suspicious. Pay close attention to messages that contain:

    • Threats or urgent demands, like “Do this now or we’ll close your account.”
    • Requests for money or promises of gifts.
    • Asks for passwords, account details, or other personal information.
    • Language that urges you to click on a link.
    • Messages from someone you don’t personally know.
    • Receiving emails from unfamiliar senders.

  • Take a close look at the email address or phone number sending you the message. When you get a request or notification regarding your account, it’s important to make sure it’s coming from a legitimate source. Scammers frequently use deceptive email addresses that closely resemble official support accounts, but they are not legitimate.

    Any correspondence from Facebook or Meta will only come from one of these email domains, or any subdomains of the following (such as support.facebook.com or business.fb.com):

    • fb.com
    • facebook.com
    • facebookmail.com
    • instagram.com
    • meta.com
    • metamail.com

    Learn more about why you are receiving email notifications from Facebookmail.com and Metamail.com.

  • Be careful what you share with others (online or in person). We recommend that you never provide your Facebook username or password to any unfamiliar source. We will never ask you for your username or password in an email message, or send you a password to verify in an attachment. Avoid responding to messages requesting personal details like social security or banking information, even if they claim to be from Facebook.

  • Be aware that fraudulent links and requests can come through various digital channels. This includes email messages, Instagram direct messages or Messenger chats. Meta representatives will never request money or ask for passwords, payment details or other sensitive information over chat or email.

    Learn what to do if you received a suspicious email or message that looks like it came from Facebook.

  • Set up two-factor authentication to help keep your account secure.

I can’t report a message

This is about using messages on Facebook. For help with the Messenger app, visit the Messenger Help Center.

If you think a message you’ve received on Facebook is spam or goes against our Community Standards, you can report the conversation.

Report a conversation on Facebook

  1. In the top right of your Facebook account, click .
  2. Open the conversation that you want to report.
  3. At the top, click the person or chat’s name or .
  4. Scroll down and click Report.
  5. Select a category to help us understand what’s wrong.
  6. Click Done.

We won’t let the person know who reported them.

Remember that not everything that may be upsetting violates our Community Standards. Community Standards violations include:

  • Bullying or harassment: Content that appears to purposefully target a person with the intention of degrading or shaming them, or repeatedly contacting a person despite that person’s clear desire and action to prevent contact.
  • Direct threats: Serious threats of harm to public and personal safety, credible threats of physical harm, specific threats of theft, vandalism, or other financial harm.
  • Sexual violence and exploitation: Content that threatens or promotes sexual violence or exploitation, including solicitation of sexual material, any sexual content involving minors, threats to share intimate things you want to keep private (such as images or videos), and offers of sexual services.
  • Impersonation: Accounts that pretend to be you or someone else.
  • Restricted goods and services: Attempts to buy, sell or trade high-risk or non-medical drugs.

A report won’t be created for technical problems and false information categories.

Learn more about Facebook safety tools and resources. If you ever feel like you or someone you know is in immediate danger, contact your local law enforcement.

If someone is bothering you on Facebook, you can always block messages from them or block their profile on Facebook.

How do I report a Page?

If you can’t access the Page you want to report, consider asking a friend to report it.

Report convicted sex offenders on Facebook

Report a sex offender

What information do I need?

Contact law enforcement

Convicted sex offenders aren’t allowed to use Facebook. If you’ve seen an account that may belong to a convicted sex offender, report it to us.

Make sure you provide one of the following types of information with your report:

  • A link to a listing in a national or state sex offender registry
  • A link to an online news article
  • A link to a court document

If you aren’t able to include this information with your report, we recommend that you ask a local law enforcement representative to contact us so we can take action on your report. Once we confirm someone’s status as a sex offender, we will immediately disable their account.

Report someone under the minimum age on Facebook

Report underage account

Minimum age for Facebook

Delete underage account

The minimum age to use Facebook varies by region. Most countries and states require you to be at least 13 years old to use Facebook. Some countries and states have different minimum age requirements:

  • South Korea: 14 years old.
  • Quebec, Canada: 14 years old.
  • Spain: 14 years old.
  • Florida, USA: 14 years old.
  • Australia: 16 years old

In some regions, you may be required to confirm your age before you can use, or continue to use, Facebook.

If you’d like to report an account belonging to someone under the minimum age to use Facebook, or if you believe someone is impersonating someone under the minimum age, please fill out this form. We will delete the account if we can’t verify that the account is managed by someone who is old enough to use Facebook. If your child created an account on Facebook, you can show them how to delete their account.

We ask for and use age-related information from people using our platform for age verification and other purposes, including to help ensure compliance with our Terms of Service. These initiatives are part of our efforts to promote safety, security and integrity. Learn more about how we work to keep Meta a safe place for everyone.

Safety resources & ways to stay safe on Facebook

Adjust my privacy settings

Report suspicious content

Recognize sensitive content

Here are a few things you can do to stay safe on Facebook:

  1. Learn how to use Facebook’s settings to comfortably share and connect with others.
  2. Learn how to recognize sensitive content and behavior and how to report it.
  3. Remember these simple rules about staying safe online:
    • Never share your password.
    • Think before you post.
    • Adjust your privacy settings and review them often.
    • Only accept friend requests from people you know personally.
    • Report things that look suspicious.

Learn more about internet safety from these resources:

  • Facebook’s Bullying Prevention Hub provides resources and tips that help teens, parents and educators deal with bullying and its consequences.
  • MTV’s A Thin Line: This campaign empowers kids to identify, respond to and stop the spread of digital abuse in their own lives. The campaign is built on the understanding that there’s a “thin line” between what may begin as a harmless joke and something that could end up having a serious impact.
  • Child Exploitation and Online Protection Centre (CEOP) works to track and bring offenders to account either directly or in partnership with local and international forces.
  • Childnet International works to track and bring offenders to account either directly or in partnership with local and international forces.
  • Commonsense.org provides trustworthy information and education to help kids thrive in a world of media and technology.
  • ConnectSafely.org is an online forum that gives teens and parents a voice in the public discussion about youth online. It also offers many other resources, such as social-media safety tips for teens and parents.
  • Cyberbullying Research Center provides up-to-date information about cyberbullying among adolescents and serves as a center of information about the ways adolescents use and misuse technology.
  • FOSI.org works to make the online world safer for families by encouraging best practices and tools that respect free expression in the field of online safety.
  • NCMEC.org serves as the US’s resource on missing and sexually exploited children. It provides information and resources to law enforcement and other professionals, parents and children, including child victims.
  • OnguardOnline.gov is a program of the US’s Federal Trade Commission that provides practical tips to avoid internet fraud.
  • UK Council for Internet Safety is a collection of research about internet safety.
  • WiredSafety has tools to help young people make smart media and technology choices. Three of their popular programs are STOP cyberbullying, Teenangels and WiredCops.

Safety tips for meeting someone from Facebook in person

Where should I meet?

What personal info is safe?

What if I feel unsafe?

Before meeting in person with someone you’ve talked to on Facebook, we recommend that you read the information below to help keep yourself safe. You are always the best judge of your own safety, and these guidelines are not meant to substitute for your own judgment.

When meeting someone from Facebook in person:

  • Meet and stay in public: Make sure that the meeting location is public and has other people around (example: coffee shop, shopping mall, park).
  • Familiarize yourself with the meeting spot: If possible, check out the meeting location ahead of time.
  • Don’t share personal information: Use your best judgment when communicating with the other person, and don’t share personal information like your home address.
  • Arrange your own transportation: Set up your own transportation to and from the meeting spot to make sure you have control over when you arrive and leave.
  • Tell someone about your plans: Tell a friend or family member the exact location you’re planning to meet and when you plan to be back home. Consider asking another adult to come with you.
  • Don’t forget your mobile phone: Bring your mobile phone with you and make sure the battery is charged.

If you feel uncomfortable or unsafe

If you are the victim of a crime or are in immediate danger, contact your local law enforcement for help.

If you ever feel pressured or uncomfortable, you can:

  • End the meeting and arrange your own transportation home.
  • Block anyone who makes you feel uncomfortable.
  • Report anything you think is violating our Community Standards.

Support for substance abuse

Find substance abuse help

SAMHSA National Helpline

Find drug treatment programs

If you’re concerned that you or one of your friends has a problem with substance abuse, there are things you can do to help or get help. If you or your friend is in immediate danger, call 911.

If the danger isn’t immediate:

  • Call or encourage your friend to call the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration’s (SAMHSA’s) National Helpline for free and confidential information and treatment referrals in English and Spanish:
    • 1-800-662-HELP (4357) or 1-800-487-4889 (TDD), available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, 365 days a year.
  • Take a look at, or tell your friend about SAMHSA’s Treatment Facility Locator, which provides a full list of drug and alcohol treatment programs across the United States.
  • Look into or share information about other resources that help people who want to stop using illegal drugs or misusing prescription drugs. These resources include Facing Addiction with NCADD’s Addiction Resource Hub which can help you find treatment options in your area, including resources for housing and other services.
  • Seek support for yourself or your friend by contacting a family member, friend, counselor or teacher, who may be able to provide support.
  • For more information about how you can help support your friend, visit SAMHSA.

You can read more about managing substance use in our emotional health hub.

Parents and Caregivers

If you’re a parent or caregiver concerned about a family member’s substance use, you can contact the Partnership for Drug Free Kids and connect with one of their specialists to help develop an action plan for you and your family by using one of the following methods available in English and Spanish:

  • Text a Message to 55753
  • Send an Email
  • Schedule a call

Tips for writing community notes on Facebook

Write a helpful community note

What makes a note unhelpful?

How to cite a source?

Community Notes on Facebook is currently in beta and some features might be unavailable.

If you find a bug while Community Notes is still in beta, you can report it by shaking your phone.

Community notes contributors are most likely to rate a note as helpful when it’s easy to understand, unbiased and when it links to a reliable source. Here are some tips to help you write helpful notes.

What makes a community note helpful

  • It provides a full explanation of the topic discussed in the post.
  • It’s relevant to the post or the topic discussed in the post.
  • It includes a link to a reliable source. The source should be a specific page or article, rather than a common domain, like facebook.com.
  • It uses neutral or unbiased language.
  • It’s easy to understand.

What makes a community note not helpful

  • It provides an incomplete explanation of the topic discussed in the post.
  • It’s not relevant to the post or the topic discussed in the post.
  • It includes a link to an unreliable source.
  • It includes incorrect information.
  • It’s someone’s opinion.
  • It uses biased or argumentative language.
  • It’s hard to understand.

Sports example

Helpful community note example

Criticizing how football games get officiated is as much a national pastime as watching them. But there haven’t been any announcements of any terminations of referees for corruption during the 2024 season.

Source: www.aol.com/football-ref-firings-153803155.html

☑️Cites a high-quality source

☑️Easy to understand

☑️Directly addresses the post’s claim

Not helpful community note example

People always complain about football refs and its rlly weird that no one’s been fired for corruption this season. Maybe it’s being covered up, or maybe no one cares. Officiating is just bad.

Source: aol.com

✖️Biased language

✖️Hard to understand

✖️Typos or unclear language

✖️Missing or unreliable source

Nature example

Helpful community note example

This is a common myth. Bats are not blind. They don’t have the same level of visual acuity as humans, but they have reasonably good eyesight. This, combined with echolocation (a biological sonar system), hearing and smell, means they can thrive well in all kinds of environments.

Source: www.naturefacts.com/animal-senses-bats-5434059.html

☑️Cites a high-quality source

☑️Complete explanation

☑️Easy to understand

☑️Directly addresses the post’s claim

Not helpful community note example

Bats can’t see at all, so they just FLY around using weird sounds!! Honestly, it’s obvious they’re basically blind.

Source: www.google.com

✖️Biased language

✖️Hard to understand

✖️Typos or unclear language

Use a security key to log into your Facebook account

I can’t log in with my key

How do security keys work?

My security key isn’t working

Before you can log in with a security key, you’ll first need to add it to your account as a security method.

Learn more about security keys and how they work.

Log into Facebook using your security key

  1. Go to facebook.com and enter your username and password.
  2. Click Log In.
  3. You’ll be asked to use your security key. Make sure you have your security key nearby. Click Continue.
  4. Either insert your security key into your computer and activate it by touching it, or if you have an NFC key, hold it near your computer’s sensor (the location of the NFC sensor depends on your device).
  5. Once your security key is verified, you’ll be logged in. If there was a problem verifying your security key, you’ll be prompted to try again.

I’m having trouble logging in with my security key

If you’re having trouble logging in with your security key, try the following:

  • Make sure that you’ve already registered the key to your account.
  • Update your app or browser and try again.
  • If you do not see an option to log in with your security key, your browser or device may not support security keys. You can learn more about what to do if your device or browser does not support security keys.
  • If you have a USB or lightning security key, make sure it’s plugged in correctly.
  • If your security key is touch activated, make sure to tap the sensor or button on your key when you want to activate it.
  • Move NFC keys slowly over your device near the sensor. The location of the NFC sensor depends on your device.
  • Charge Bluetooth keys regularly.
  • Check the manufacturer’s instructions for your security key for additional help.

Other Useful Resources

  • Learn how to prevent account access issues if you lose your security key by setting up alternate two factor authentication methods.
  • Your security key can be used with other websites while also being used for your Facebook account.
  • If you’re running Linux, you’ll need to follow this additional step to use your security key.

Use Crisis Response on Facebook

Request help in Crisis Response

Offer help in Crisis Response

Crisis Response guidelines

You can use Crisis Response to find help through your community for things such as transportation, food or supplies.

To request help using Crisis Response, visit Facebook on an iOS or Android device.

iPhone or iPad

  1. Tap Search in the top right of Facebook.
  2. Search and tap Crisis Response from Facebook shortcuts.
  3. Select the crisis you want to find help for.
  4. Scroll down to Community Help unit and then tap See all
  5. Tap Request or offer help.
  6. Tap Offer help or Request help.

If you find someone giving the type of help you need, comment on the post or message the person who posted to connect with them.

You can also scroll through existing posts on the Crisis page to see what types of help people in the area are offering.

Android

  1. Tap Search in the top right of Facebook.
  2. Search and tap Crisis Response from Facebook shortcuts.
  3. Select the crisis you want to find help for.
  4. Scroll down to Community Help unit and then tap See all
  5. Tap Request or offer help.
  6. Tap Offer help or Request help.

If you find someone giving the type of help you need, comment on the post or message the person who posted to connect with them.

You can also scroll through existing posts on the Crisis page to see what types of help people in the area are offering.

Crisis Response posts must follow these guidelines

  • They must follow our Community Standards.
  • They must be relevant to the crisis.
  • They can’t be promotional in nature or contain commercial offers.

If you need urgent help, please contact your local emergency services.

Why do I wait 24 hours?

I can’t log in after 24 hours

What is a security check?

After you complete a security check, you’ll have to wait 24 hours to log into your Facebook account. During this time, your account will still be visible to your friends on Facebook, but you won’t be able to access it. This waiting period is an extra security precaution we set up to protect your account and the information in it. We appreciate your patience with this security measure.

Ways to stay safe on Facebook when using Crisis Response

Meet in a safe location

Protect my privacy

Report suspicious posts

Here are some safety tips to keep in mind when requesting and offering help on Facebook in response to a crisis:

Meet in a safe location: Try to meet in a public place. Before going to an agreed upon location, tell a family member or a friend the exact place where you’ll be meeting, bring your mobile phone and consider asking someone to come with you.

Protect your privacy: People may need to share their personal information (example: mobile phone number, address) so that you can meet in person to provide assistance. Remember to always be cautious when sharing personal information with others and never share financial information.

Consider mutual friends: Before messaging someone through Crisis Response, look to see if you and the person have mutual friends on Facebook. If you do share any mutual friends, you can then check in with your friend before meeting someone you don’t know personally.

Report suspicious posts: If you see a post that looks suspicious, please report the post to Facebook for our team to review. This will help keep the community safe.

What data gets sent to Facebook when I report a problem?

What data is collected?

What are complete logs?

How long is data stored?

When you report a problem to Facebook, we automatically collect information related to the issue you’re reporting from your device, app and account.

What information does Facebook automatically collect when I report a problem?

When you report a problem, we automatically collect information such as what device you’re using, whether you’re accessing Facebook from a desktop or mobile device, what version of Facebook you have installed, your User ID, and other signals that help us understand and resolve the error, flaw, failure or other issue you experienced.

What other information can I choose to provide Facebook when I report a problem?

When you report a problem to us, you’re also given the option to help us further fix your issue by sending complete logs and diagnostics. This includes information such as user activity logs, network logs, crash logs and memory dumps associated with the app from which you reported a problem. You also have the option of including additional content within your report that you think may help us better understand the issue, such as screenshots of the problem you’re experiencing.

How long does Facebook store the information from my report?

We will store the information contained in your report only for as long as required to resolve the issue you are reporting and others like it. We will not use the information contained in your report for other purposes. Your information will be processed outside of the European Economic Area, including in the United States. To learn more about how your information is used more generally when you use this app, please see our Privacy Policy.

What happens when you report a bug or broken feature on Facebook

My report was resolved

Report a broken feature

Report account problems

What happens after I report?

When things don’t work on Facebook we want to fix them right away. As people send us reports about broken features, we review them and sometimes reach out for more information to help us resolve the problem.

If the Support Inbox status for something you reported says it was resolved but you’re still experiencing the problem, please report it again with the following tips in mind:

  • Be sure to report account problems or abusive content through the right channel.
  • Report broken features as soon as you see them.
  • Clearly explain what you were doing when the problem occurred and what steps we can take to reproduce the problem.
  • Attach screenshots if you have them.
  • The feature might actually be working as intended, so check the Help Center to see if that’s the case.

Reporting issues when they happen helps make Facebook better. We appreciate the time it takes to give us this information.

What is defamation and how do I report it on Facebook?

Report defamatory content

What is defamation?

Report criminal insult

Defamation is generally a false statement of fact that harms someone’s reputation. If you would like to report a post you believe is defamatory, you can fill out this form.

Please note that, due to local laws, this reporting form may not be available in your location. In addition, filling out a defamation report through this form doesn’t guarantee that we will restrict access to the reported content.

Certain statements may not be defamatory but may still go against our Community Standards for bullying or harassment, for example. Learn how to report violations of our Standards.

What is social reporting on Facebook

Ask friend to take down post

Report bullying or harassment

Block someone on Facebook

If you see something on Facebook that you don’t like, but it doesn’t violate the Facebook Terms or Community Standards, you can send a message to the person who posted it asking them to take it down. For example, let’s say someone posts a photo of you that you find embarrassing. You can send this person a message and let them know how this photo makes you feel. In most cases, people will take things off Facebook if a friend asks them to.

In certain cases (example: bullying or harassment) you may not feel comfortable reaching out to the person directly. In these cases, you can:

  • Report something to Facebook.
  • Share the content (example: photo, message) that’s making you uncomfortable with someone you trust, like a parent, teacher or trusted friend.
  • Block the person or unfriend the person who’s making you uncomfortable.

What security measures are in place to make sure someone else doesn’t download a copy of my Facebook information

Download my information

Secure my information download

My download link expired

What is a security challenge?

We have a number of security measures in place to help make sure you’re the only one who can download a copy of your information:

  • Once your download is ready, we’ll send an email to the primary email address listed on your Facebook account along with a link to your download. This link expires after a few days. If the link expires, you’ll have to go through the download process again.
  • We require you to enter your password before you can download the file containing your information.
  • If you’re using a public computer or one you don’t use regularly, you may also have to solve a security challenge. Note: This file may contain private information. You should keep it secure and take precautions when storing or sending it, or uploading it to another service.

What should I do if I’m getting warnings from my computer’s anti-virus software after accessing an app on Facebook?

Report a Facebook app

Remove a Facebook app

My computer has a virus

Facebook works to ensure that all developers are following our policies. If you receive warnings for an app that you’re trying to access via Facebook, please report the app.

When you report it, please select the problem that most closely matches your experience with the app. We’ll investigate your report and take appropriate action based on our Platform Policy.

Keep in mind that apps on Facebook Platform are maintained by developers outside of Facebook, and they can link to content outside of Facebook. We recommend that you keep your anti-virus software up-to-date and run its virus removal feature if you think your computer may have been infected. You can also remove or restrict apps.

Why didn’t Facebook remove the content that I reported

Request another review

I disagree with a decision

Appeal to Oversight Board

How long does review take?

When you report a piece of content (example: photo, comment, post) to us, we will take action to hide or remove the content from Facebook if we find that it goes against our Community Standards. Our Community Standards define what is and isn’t allowed on Facebook, and they apply all over the world. They’re designed to encourage expression and create a safe environment on Facebook.

After you report a piece of content, you’ll receive a notification in your Support Inbox, where you can check the status of something you’ve reported to us. After we review the content, we’ll let you know whether it did or did not go against our Community Standards.

What if I disagree with Facebook’s decision regarding content I reported?

We will remove content when we find it goes against our Community Standards. If you report content by others but we find the content does not go against our Community Standards, we will let you know. At that time, if you disagree with our decision to leave the content up, we usually offer the chance for you to request another review. When you request another review, we’ll revisit the content and review it again. For some types of content, you can’t request another review but we’re adding more options.

Request another review of the content you reported

  1. Click your profile picture in the top right of Facebook.
  2. Select Help & support.
  3. Click Support Inbox.
  4. Click Reports About Others.
  5. Open the message we sent you about our decision on the content you reported.
  6. Click See Options at the bottom.
  7. If the option is available, click Request another review and follow the on-screen instructions.

Once you ask us to take another look, your content will be reviewed again, usually within 24 hours. If we find we’ve made a mistake, we’ll let you know and the content you reported will be hidden or removed.

If you’ve requested another review and we uphold our decision for the second time, you may be able to appeal the decision to the Oversight Board. Keep in mind that not all decisions are eligible for appeal to the Oversight Board and the board only selects a certain number of eligible appeals, so they may not choose yours to review. You can read more about the board’s bylaws and structure on their website.

Search on Facebook

Filter my search results

Search for something

  1. Click Search in the top left of any page on Facebook.
  2. Enter what you’re looking for and choose from the results.

When typing something, you may see predictions for what you’re looking for. If you see what you’re looking for in these predictions, click it to save time searching.

Filter your search results

  1. Click Search in the top left of any page on Facebook, then type something into the search bar or select a search prediction.
  2. Click a filter in the left column (example: People, Photos) to narrow your search.

Use keywords in search

Search supports keyword searches to help you find what you’re looking for on Facebook. When you start searching with keywords (example: “Caroline wedding” or “cookie recipe Lisa”) you’ll see results that you can filter.

You can also select one of the predicted searches to see a full list of search options for that prediction.

What can I search for on Facebook?

Search for people

Search for posts

Search for photos

Facebook search results are based on your Facebook activity. Facebook search results aren’t influenced by activity off Facebook.

You can search for people, posts, photos, videos, places, Pages, groups, apps, links, events and more on Facebook. Start searching with keywords (example: Caroline wedding) and you’ll see a list of results that you can filter. If you need some ideas, you can try some of these searches:

John Smith Chicago pizza

Cookie recipe Lisa

Hawaii hotel

You can also combine phrases together, or add things like locations, times, likes and interests to get more specific (example: friends who live in San Francisco).

Keep in mind that Facebook search results are ranked based on a combination of your activity on Facebook and that of the Facebook community in general. What appears in search results is content that was posted directly on Facebook.

What shows up in Facebook search results?

What influences my search results?

Why do I see public posts?

How to get non-personalized results?

You can search for people, posts, photos, videos, places, Pages, groups, apps, links, events and more on Facebook. Facebook search results are based on your Facebook activity. Facebook search results aren’t influenced by activity off Facebook.

Your unique Facebook search results are based on Facebook activity such as:

  • What you’re able to see on Facebook, including what your friends share with you.
  • Posts from your friends.
  • Places where you’ve been tagged or places similar to those places.
  • Things you like (example: Pages you follow or interests indicated on your profile).
  • Groups you’ve joined.
  • Events you’ve liked or are interested in.
  • Previous searches you’ve done.
  • Content you’ve interacted with in News Feed.

Your Facebook search results are also based on Facebook community activity including:

  • Popularity of content for a particular search term.
  • How recently something was posted.

You may see results from people you’re not friends with because you’re in the audience for the post. Keep in mind that public posts can be seen by anyone, including people outside of Facebook.

See stories on Messenger

You can see stories of people, Pages you follow and suggested stories using the Facebook app or on facebook.com from your computer and mobile browser. You can also see stories of people you’re connected with on Messenger. If a person or Page has shared a story you haven’t seen yet, you’ll see a blue ring around their profile picture.

Keep in mind that when you view a story, the account (including account owners and admins) that created the story will be able to tell that you’ve seen it.

Using the Facebook app

Stories appear in a row at the top of your Feed. If someone you’re friends with or a Page you follow has posted a story, you can see it by doing any of the following options:

  • Tap their story at the top of Feed.
  • Go to their profile or Page and tap their profile picture.
  • Tap their profile picture next to a post they’ve shared in Feed.

Stories may also appear in other places on the Facebook app, such as your Feed. For stories in your Feed, if you stop to view, react or reply to the story the story’s creator will be able to tell that you’ve seen it.

On facebook.com

Stories appear at the top of Feed on your computer and mobile browser. Tap or click on any story to view it, or use the arrows (computer) or swipe left (mobile) to get to the next screen or story. Tap or click in the top left to exit someone’s story and return to Feed.

You can also view someone’s story by going to their profile or Page, scrolling to their most recent post and tapping or clicking on their profile picture.

Using the Messenger app

Stories can be seen within the Messenger app for iPhone and Android. If someone you’re friends with or connected with on Messenger has posted a story, you can see it.

To see someone’s story on Messenger for Android:

  1. Tap Stories at the bottom.
  2. Tap their story.

Swipe down on the screen or tap in the top right to exit someone’s story and return to Messenger.

You can delete a collection from your Featured section or remove photos or stories from a collection. When you remove photos and stories from your Featured section, it doesn’t delete the original photo or story:

Share story to Instagram

We’re gradually updating people to Meta Accounts. You may see either Accounts Center or Meta Account settings as the place to manage your account settings.

When you share something to your story, it can appear in a number of places, such as:

  • At the top of Facebook Feed: Your story will appear at the top of your friends’ or followers’ Feed on Facebook. At the top of your own Feed, your story will be the first story in this section.
  • At the top of Messenger: Your story will appear in a row at the top of your Messenger inbox.
  • In Feed: Your story may appear in your friends’ or followers’ Feed. If they stop to view, react or reply to your story, you’ll be able to tell that they viewed it.
  • On Instagram: If you’ve added your accounts to the same Accounts Center as your Instagram account, you can share your story to your Instagram account. Your Instagram privacy settings will apply to your stories shared from Instagram.

Your stories will be visible to your selected audience for 24 hours. Any photos or videos you add to your story on Facebook will also appear in your story on Messenger.

Note: If you share your Instagram story to Facebook, it will also appear as a story at the top of your Feed in Facebook, in the Messenger app and it may appear in your friends’ or followers’ Feed. Keep in mind that any Instagram story you share to Facebook and Messenger will use your existing story privacy settings you’ve chosen in the Facebook or Messenger app.

Supervision and Family Center

About Facebook Teen Accounts

Set up supervision

Manage my teen’s time

Change teen account settings

Teen Accounts and some of its protections are currently being rolled out on an individual basis, which means parents and guardians may have a teen who has a Teen Account or additional protections before their other teens do.

Teen Accounts limit who can contact teens on Messenger. Learn more about Teen Accounts on Messenger.

Teen Accounts are Facebook accounts for teens 13-17 that are automatically set to protective account settings. These settings aim to help keep teens safe on Facebook by limiting unwanted contact and helping them manage their time on Facebook.

Supervision

A parent or guardian must supervise their teen’s account before they can:

  • Manage their teen’s time on Facebook with daily limit and sleep mode.
  • Approve or deny their teen’s request to make certain settings less protective.
  • See contacts their teen has added, including Facebook friends, Messenger connections and AIs they’ve chatted with.
  • Allow teens to manage their own settings without requiring parental approvals.

Learn how to set up supervision on Facebook.

Teen Account settings

Teens under 16 need their parent’s or guardian’s permission if they wish to update these settings to be less protective. Teens 16-17 can change most of these settings themselves, unless their account is supervised by a parent or guardian. These settings include:

Content setting

The Teen Accounts content setting is automatically set to Ages 13+. This means we work to hide more content that may be inappropriate for people under 18. Their ability to message or interact with profiles and Pages that primarily share content that may be inappropriate for teens will also be limited. Teens 13-17 need permission from their parent or guardian to change this setting to More content.

Audience settings

The following audience settings will automatically be set to Friends for Teen Accounts. Teens will be notified 7 days before the change happens.

  • Who can see your future posts, stories or reels
  • Who can see your friends list
  • Who can see people, Pages and lists you follow
  • Who can see posts you’re tagged in on your profile
  • Who can comment on your public posts

The following audience settings will be automatically set to the most protective setting:

  • Review posts you’re tagged in before the post appears on their profile: Automatically set to on for new accounts.
  • Allow anyone to remix your future public reels: Automatically set to off for new accounts.

Profile details teens 13-15 need permission to update:

The following profile settings will be automatically set to Only me for Teen Accounts. This means only the teen can see the following profile information.

  • Phone number
  • Email address

The following profile settings will automatically be set to Friends for Teen Accounts. This means only the teen’s Facebook Friends can see the following profile information. Teens 16-17 can update these settings themselves.

  • Birthday
  • Birth year

Profile detail settings teens 13-15 don’t need permission to update:

Teens 13-15 will be able to adjust some Profile detail settings themselves, without parental permission. These settings include:

  • Relationship status: Who can see this setting will automatically be set to Friends.
  • Work: Who can see this setting will automatically be set to Friends of friends.
  • Education: Who can see this setting will automatically be set to Friends of friends.

Note: if teens already have more protective audience and profile details setting selections than the Teen Account defaults, their settings won’t change with the introduction of Teen Accounts.

Sleep Mode and Daily Limit

  • Sleep mode: Teen Accounts automatically have sleep mode turned on from 10PM to 7AM every day. During sleep mode, Facebook notifications are muted and the teen will see a reminder to close Facebook.
  • Daily limit: Teen Accounts automatically get a reminder to close Facebook after a total of 1 hour is spent on Facebook each day.

If you’re a teen, learn more about managing your Teen Account settings. If you’re a teen with pro mode, learn more about how your settings can affect the tools available to you.

If you’re a parent, learn more about supporting your teen on Facebook.

If you have a Teen Account and are 18 or older, you can edit your birthday in your settings. Learn more about editing or adding a birthday on Facebook.

Note: Teen Accounts profile and audience settings will not affect teens’ participation in Groups or Pages. If teens use Groups or Pages to view or share content, they may be subject to the audience models for Groups and Pages.

Teen Accounts may not be compatible with older versions of Facebook. Try updating your Facebook app if you’re having issues managing your Teen Account.
